data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001's core claim—that a monolith can enforce homogeneous fault domains to reduce correlated-failure risk—assumes the very condition the problem asks the target to earn: that a homogeneous fault domain is more resilient under correlated failure than a distributed one. But a homogeneous fault domain is a textbook common-mode coupling amplifier. If every internal replica shares the same build toolchain, scheduler, config daemon, and validation logic, then a latent bug anywhere in that shared stack becomes a single ancestor whose activation fails the entire 'strictly more redundant' service at once. The Y2K analogy the target itself imports proves the opposite of the claim: Y2K was catastrophic precisely because systems were homogeneous in their calendar encoding. Yet the target insists homogeneous fault domains are safer from correlated failure, while the only analogy it offers shows homogeneity enabling the largest correlated failure. It concedes the shared-cause is 'typically unknown' in the decentralized case, which means the monolith's internal coupling is similarly hidden until triggered—the shared-ancestor tail is just internal rather than external. Thus the 'monolith wins by enforcing homogeneous fault domains' premise is in direct tension with the common-mode coupling principle the problem demands, and the target never reconciles it.
